title: Validate Binary Search Tree
description: A common trap solved correctly: why checking only the direct parent fails, and the fix via recursive inherited bounds.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given the root of a binary tree, determine if it is a valid binary search tree (BST): for every node, all values in its left subtree are strictly less than the node's value, and all values in its right subtree are strictly greater.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","root of a binary tree"],["Output","true if it satisfies the BST property everywhere, false otherwise"],["Key Insight","Each node must respect bounds inherited from ALL ancestors, not just its direct parent"],["Constraints","Up to 10^4 nodes"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Every node in the left subtree less than the root, every node in the right subtree greater\"","A recursive bounds-passing technique: each recursive call carries a valid (low, high) range that the current node must fall strictly within"]]}

blocks.text: A common mistake is checking only whether a node's value is greater than its immediate left child and less than its immediate right child; this misses violations from further up the tree. The BST property is GLOBAL: a node deep in a left subtree must still be less than some ancestor several levels up, not just its direct parent.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Nested Set of Fences, Each Narrower Than the Last
blocks.text: Picture walking down a tree where every step down narrows an allowed range like nested fences: going left narrows the allowed range's upper bound to the current value, going right narrows the lower bound, and every node must stay strictly within the CURRENT nested fence, not just avoid its direct neighbors.

blocks.caption: A node must respect bounds inherited from every ancestor, not just its direct parent

blocks.text: Valid = false. Node 3 (under 4, under 5) is less than its parent 4, but violates the inherited bound from ancestor 5 (must be greater than 5, since it is in 5's right subtree, but 3 is less than 5).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Checking a node only against its direct parent is insufficient, since a node several levels down must still respect bounds set by ancestors much higher up.

Observation 2: As the recursion descends, going into a LEFT child narrows the upper bound to the current node's value (everything in a left subtree must be less than that value); going into a RIGHT child narrows the lower bound similarly.

Observation 3: Passing an accumulated (low, high) range down through the recursion, and checking each node strictly falls within it, correctly enforces the GLOBAL constraint from every ancestor, not just the direct parent.
This leads to a recursive function carrying a valid (low, high) range downward, narrowing it appropriately at each left or right step.
Check each node only against its direct parent (comparing the parent-child relationship locally), missing constraints inherited from further up the tree.
Why the code is written this way

items: Comparing only against the direct parent seems intuitive but is actually INCORRECT, not just inefficient, since it misses constraints from higher ancestors.
This is included specifically as a common trap: the real fix requires tracking an inherited range, not a single parent comparison.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), but INCORRECT results on trees where a deeper node violates a higher ancestor's bound.
Space: O(h) recursion depth.
Limitation: this approach is not just slower, it is WRONG; passing an accumulated (low, high) range down through the recursion is required for correctness, not merely for efficiency.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Define valid(node, lo, hi) recursively: an empty node is trivially valid. Otherwise, the current node's value must be STRICTLY between lo and hi; if not, return false immediately. Recursively check valid(node.left, lo, node.val) (narrowing the upper bound to the current value) AND valid(node.right, node.val, hi) (narrowing the lower bound to the current value). Start the top-level call with lo as negative infinity and hi as positive infinity.
Use a recursive bounds-passing check: each node must strictly fall within its inherited (low, high) range, narrowed appropriately going left or right.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Node","Bounds (lo, hi)","Valid?"],"rows":[["5 (root)","(-inf, inf)","yes"],["1 (left of 5)","(-inf, 5)","yes"],["4 (right of 5)","(5, inf)","FAILS, 4 is not greater than 5"]]}

blocks.text: Passing an accumulated (low, high) range down through the recursion correctly encodes EVERY ancestor's constraint simultaneously: going left narrows the allowed upper bound to the current value (since everything further left must stay below it), and going right narrows the allowed lower bound similarly, so by the time any node is checked, its (low, high) range already reflects every relevant ancestor, not just its direct parent.

blocks.text: Validate Binary Search Tree is a classic trap problem: the naive "check against the direct parent" approach is not just suboptimal, it is incorrect, and recognizing the need for GLOBAL inherited bounds is the key insight.

items: Checking only the direct parent-child relationship, missing violations from higher ancestors, a genuinely incorrect (not just inefficient) approach.
Using non-strict inequalities (allowing equal values) when the BST property requires strict less-than and greater-than relationships.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A tree with duplicate values","Invalid, since the BST property requires strict inequality, not allowing equal values."],["A single node tree","Always valid trivially."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "checking only the direct parent is not enough, bounds must be inherited from every ancestor" heads off the most common mistake on this problem before writing any code.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "validate that a tree satisfies the BST property", think: recursive bounds-passing with an inherited (low, high) range, not a local parent comparison.

items: How would you validate this using an inorder traversal instead, checking that values are strictly increasing?

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The naive direct-parent check is INCORRECT regardless of its O(n) time; the bounds-passing approach costs the same O(n) time but is actually correct, the standard solution.

items: Pattern: recursive bounds-passing, carrying an inherited (low, high) range down through the tree.
Core Idea: going left narrows the upper bound to the current value; going right narrows the lower bound; every node must strictly fall within its inherited range.
Most Important Observation: checking only the direct parent is a genuine bug, not merely an inefficiency.
Interview Difficulty: a classic medium problem with a well-known trap.
One line memory trick: bounds narrow as you descend, inherited from every ancestor.
